candidates.attacker_control: Full control of the XML document supplied to XStream.fromXML(String/Reader/InputStream/File/URL) or unmarshal(...). Element node names, the system attributes 'class', 'resolves-to' and 'defined-in', every field/property name and every value are attacker-chosen. These strings select the Java classes to load, instantiate and populate, and the object graph fed to class-defined callbacks (e.g. handler class and interfaces of a <dynamic-proxy>, the object stream consumed by readExternal).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that no security layer exists in the snapshot: searches for TypePermission, allowTypes, denyType, ForbiddenClassException and blacklist return nothing; no com.thoughtworks.xstream.security package exists; Mapper.shouldSerializeMember in DefaultMapper.java:115-117 always returns true. Confirmed the snapshot is release 1.4.6 (pom.xml:23,110; xstream/pom.xml:17; xstream-distribution/src/content/changes.html ends at 1.4.6), i.e. before the fix. Considered the project's own contract in the docs: the 1.4.6 documentation contains no warning that untrusted input must not be unmarshalled and provides no allow/deny API, so no documented trust boundary is contradicted. Considered that the default driver is XppDriver, not DomDriver, which does not mitigate this finding because type resolution/instantiation is driver-independent. Considered instantiation limits (PureJavaReflectionProvider needs a no-arg constructor or Serializable; Sun14ReflectionProvider uses Unsafe), which narrow gadget choice but not the root cause.
candidates.impact: Remote code execution in the JVM of any application that deserializes untrusted XML with XStream 1.4.6: an attacker who controls the document can make the library load, instantiate and populate arbitrary classes and trigger their deserialization callbacks/comparators, which converts XML parsing into arbitrary method invocation (process launch in the classic chain). Even without a full RCE gadget, the same missing restriction permits arbitrary object-graph construction and side effects in converters (file/URL handling, reflection, resource exhaustion).
candidates.prerequisites: (1) Application unmarshals XML that an attacker can influence with a stock XStream 1.4.6 instance (the default XStream() constructor, XStream.java:339-341, uses XppDriver and the default mapper chain; no allowTypes/denyTypes API exists in this snapshot to constrain it). (2) A gadget type reachable from JDK/application classpath that performs a dangerous action when constructed/populated or when one of its serialization methods or comparator methods is invoked (JDK-only building blocks available here are e.g. java.beans.EventHandler combined with DynamicProxyConverter, or classes with readObject/readExternal/readResolve side effects). (3) The configured reflection provider can instantiate the selected class (Sun14ReflectionProvider is used by default on supported JVMs and can bypass constructors via Unsafe).
candidates.root_cause: The unmarshalling pipeline places no restriction on which classes may be referenced by the XML. HierarchicalStreams.readClassType() takes the root element name or the class/resolves-to/defined-in attributes straight from the document and hands them to Mapper.realClass(); DefaultMapper.realClass() performs Class.forName() on that attacker string. Converters then instantiate and populate the resulting types (AbstractReflectionConverter.instantiateNewInstance/newInstance; PureJavaReflectionProvider.newInstance uses setAccessible(true)+Constructor.newInstance; Sun14ReflectionProvider uses Unsafe.allocateInstance) and execute class-defined behaviour (readResolve/readObject/readExternal, InvocationHandler creation). No TypePermission/allowTypes/blacklist mechanism exists anywhere in the snapshot, and Mapper.shouldSerializeMember() unconditionally returns true (DefaultMapper.shouldSerializeMember), so there is no allow/deny check to bypass or misuse - the capability itself is unrestricted.
candidates.title: Unrestricted attacker-controlled type instantiation during XML unmarshalling in XStream 1.4.6 (remote code execution class, CVE-2013-7285 root cause)
candidates.trace: XStream.fromXML(String) (XStream.java:1002-1003) -> fromXML(Reader) -> unmarshal(reader, null) -> unmarshal(reader, root, dataHolder) (XStream.java:1155-1160) -> marshalling strategy -> TreeUnmarshaller.start() (core/TreeUnmarshaller.java:131-141) -> HierarchicalStreams.readClassType() (core/util/HierarchicalStreams.java:25-34) reads the root element name or 'class'/'resolves-to' attribute -> Mapper.realClass() -> DefaultMapper.realClass() -> Class.forName(elementName, initialize, classLoader) (mapper/DefaultMapper.java:63-81). The resolved Class selects the converter; AbstractReflectionConverter.unmarshal() then calls instantiateNewInstance() (AbstractReflectionConverter.java:254-258, 542-555) which resolves the attacker-controlled 'resolves-to' value as a class and calls ReflectionProvider.newInstance() (PureJavaReflectionProvider.java:59-70: setAccessible(true)+Constructor.newInstance; or Sun14ReflectionProvider.java:62-75: unsafe.allocateInstance), after which fields are populated reflectively from the document and callReadResolve() is invoked (SerializationMethodInvoker.java:58-78). Nested elements repeat the cycle, and dedicated converters turn declarative XML into executable structure: DynamicProxyConverter.unmarshal() reads the interface list and the handler class from the document and builds a java.lang.reflect.Proxy whose InvocationHandler is an attacker-selected object (DynamicProxyConverter.java:100-135); ExternalizableConverter.unmarshal() constructs the attacker-named Externalizable type and calls readExternal() with an ObjectInput whose readFromStream() resolves further class names from XML (ExternalizableConverter.java:115-152); SerializationMethodInvoker can invoke readResolve()/readObject() on deserialized objects (SerializationMethodInvoker.java:109-123). During collection population, TreeMapConverter.unmarshalComparator()/populateTreeMap() install the attacker-supplied comparator and add entries, causing comparator.compare()/Comparable.compareTo() to be invoked on the attacker-built proxy (TreeMapConverter.java:104-133; TreeSetConverter.java:58-96), which is how a DynamicProxyConverter+EventHandler object graph is driven to call an arbitrary target method (e.g. ProcessBuilder.start) before unmarshalling even returns.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no runtime exploit was attempted; exploitability is inferred from source. Availability of a specific gadget class in a given deployment is assumed, not proven. The application-side fact that untrusted XML reaches fromXML/unmarshal is a usage precondition, not visible in this library-only snapshot (no test sources are present). The relation index has no data-flow/control-flow analysis and 1 unparsed Java file, so a small number of edges could not be cross-checked.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data (unsafe polymorphic type resolution/instantiation)

coverage_summary: Model-visible scope is 406 files (355 Java) across the xstream core module, xstream-benchmark and xstream-hibernate modules, plus Maven build files and distribution documentation; the P1 relation index reports 406/406 files indexed, 0 omitted, 1 parse error, 4145 symbols and 8016 edges, with no control-flow, data-flow or semantic resolution and only name/arity-based call and inheritance candidates. I read and verified the core unmarshalling and type-resolution path (XStream.java entry points, core/TreeUnmarshaller, core/util/HierarchicalStreams, mapper/DefaultMapper, mapper/Mapper/MapperWrapper, all reflection converters including AbstractReflectionConverter, PureJavaReflectionProvider, Sun14ReflectionProvider, SerializationMethodInvoker, ExternalizableConverter, DynamicProxyConverter, SerializableConverter key regions), the collection converters that invoke comparators (TreeMapConverter, TreeSetConverter, PresortedMap), representative XML/JSON I/O drivers (DomDriver, StaxDriver, XppReader), and the persistence package; I also searched globally for command-execution, URL-connection, security-framework and XML-parser-hardening patterns. Coverage is not exhaustive: the benchmark module, xstream-hibernate converters, distribution HTML/docs and large parts of XStream.java were only skimmed or searched rather than line-by-line reviewed, and one Java file failed to parse in the index (identity not reported by the index).
limitations: Static, read-only review: no compilation, tests, scanners or exploit payloads were run; the finding is a source-evidenced lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.

The P1 index explicitly lacks control-flow and data-flow analysis and semantic resolution; its call/inheritance edges are name/arity-based candidates only, so reachability of every path above was verified by reading source, not by the index.
The snapshot contains no test sources (no src/test tree), so intended usage/trust model could only be inferred from library code and the 1.4.6 documentation bundled in the repository.
One Java file is reported unparsed by the relation index; its identity is not exposed, so relations to/from it may be missing.
Gadget-class availability on a real classpath and the application's willingness to unmarshal untrusted XML are deployment preconditions outside this snapshot and were not verified.
Binary-like files are refused by the read tools; the scope report lists 0 excluded binary files, but any such content could not be inspected.

rejected_leads.lead: XML External Entity (XXE) in DomDriver: DomDriver() creates a DocumentBuilderFactory with no hardening (DomDriver.java:64) and parses attacker XML via newDocumentBuilder().parse(source) (DomDriver.java:92-98), so external entities/DTD resolution are parser-default. StaxDriver.createInputFactory() (StaxDriver.java:240-242) is likewise unconfigured.
rejected_leads.reason: Real weakness in this version, but not selected: DomDriver is not the default driver (XStream.java:339-341 uses XppDriver) so it requires an explicit driver choice, impact (file disclosure/SSRF) is lower than the deserialization RCE, and only one candidate may be submitted. Left as an unconfirmed lead.

rejected_leads.lead: FilePersistenceStrategy.extractKey() resolves class names from persistence file names via mapper.realClass() (FilePersistenceStrategy.java:88-107) and readFile() unmarshals those files with xstream.fromXML() (AbstractFilePersistenceStrategy.java:161-178).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires an attacker to already be able to create/rename files inside the configured persistence directory; the derived class from a file name is then deflected through a SingleValueConverter, so it is a less direct and weaker variant of the same deserialization root cause. Not separately reported.

rejected_leads.lead: Resource-consumption/DoS and side-effect converters (deeply nested XML, File/URL/Charset/Font/Color converters) on attacker input.
rejected_leads.reason: Generic robustness issues without a demonstrated security-specific trust-boundary violation; not sufficient evidence for a separate candidate.

summary: Snapshot is XStream 1.4.6 (pom.xml / xstream/pom.xml declare 1.4.6 and the change log ends at 1.4.6), i.e. the release that still has no type-permission/security layer on the unmarshalling path. I traced the full XML-to-object path and confirmed that element names and class/resolves-to attributes are resolved to arbitrary classes (Class.forName), that those classes are instantiated and populated by the converters, and that converter side effects (dynamic-proxy InvocationHandler, Externalizable.readExternal / Serializable readObject, readResolve, comparator invocation while populating sorted collections) are driven entirely by attacker-controlled XML. The single strongest candidate is this unrestricted type-driven deserialization (CWE-502), which is the root cause of the remote-code-execution class assigned to this version. A second real issue (unconfigured XML parsers in DomDriver/StaxDriver enabling XXE) is noted as a viable but not selected lead, since it is lower impact and not the default driver path. No runtime confirmation was performed; exploitability requires an application that unmarshals untrusted XML and a usable gadget class on the classpath.
